## Pareto Optimal Plans {#sec-algorithm}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Computing the Pareto front exactly, its complexity, and the ZenoSolver with its certificates and their verification
:::

We now focus on finding the Pareto Optimal Plans from the lists of $2t - p$ cities, for the
symmetric case: (S) holds throughout, and the statements about the front also need (A1) or, by
{{< node "Corollary 4.12" >}}, (AΔ). This section corresponds to §7 to §9 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md). The
[algorithm page](../solver/algorithm.qmd) of the Solver section describes how the implementation
carries out each step.

### Definitions {#sec-definitions}

**Cost of a list**: Given a list $X$ of $2t - p$ cities, the cost of any plan using only the
cities in $X$ is uniquely defined by $c(X) = \sum_{i \in X} c_i$.

**Makespan of a list**: The makespan of a list is that of the shortest schedule that uses its
cities in a feasible way. Only the least largest load $M(X) = \min \max_k \ell(X_k)$ over the
admissible partitions of $X$ matters: by Theorem 4.1 it is the makespan of a schedule that never
waits, and by Corollary 4.8, under (A1) or (AΔ), the Pareto front is the Pareto set of the pairs
$(c(X), M(X))$.

The list $X$ does not hold any information about which plane will land in a particular city, and
choosing the partition is the hard part.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 8.1" >}} Deciding $M(X) \le 2T$, with $d$, $X$, $p$ and $T$ as input, is
strongly NP-complete.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Reduce from 3-Partition: $3m$ cities of durations $a_i$, each once in $X$, $p = m$ and
$t = 2m$. Every group is then odd by {{< node "Lemma 2.4" badge=false >}}, and groups of duration
at most $B$ summing to $mB$ must be triples
({{< node "Theorem 8.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 8.2" >}} **Fixed $p$.** For $p = 2$ the problem stays NP-complete, even
with positive durations. For every fixed $p$ it is solvable in time polynomial in $n$, $s$ and
$T$, so for fixed $p$ it is weakly NP-complete.
:::

In particular, no greedy distribution of the durations of a list into $p$ planes is optimal in
general, unless P = NP. Distributing the longest durations first, each to the plane with the
smallest current duration, misses front points ({{< node "§5" >}}). With two cities of durations
6 and 10, two planes and five passengers, take the list of $2t - p = 8$ cities with three landings
in the slow city and five in the fast one. The greedy gives each plane a pattern $A$ in the slow
city first and ends with durations 52 and 68, while the groups $\{10, 10, 10\}$ and
$\{6, 6, 6, 6, 6\}$, both odd and hence admissible, both last 60; the front point $(260, 60)$ of
that instance is missed. The experiment [E10](#sec-e10) measures how often such a
greedy is exact.

The method below never computes $M(X)$ for a fixed list. It sweeps the makespans instead, and
computes for each one the least cost over all lists at once.

### Computing the Pareto front {#sec-breakpoints}

Scale the durations to integers and divide them by their gcd $g$. For an integer *level*
$T \ge 0$ let
$$E(T) = \min\{c(X) : |X| = 2t - p,\ X_1, \dots, X_p \text{ admissible},\ \delta(X_k) \le T \text{ for all } k\},$$
the least cost of an admissible partition whose loads are all at most $2T$. $E$ is non-increasing,
and the relaxation $L$ of {{< node "Lemma 3.4" >}} is the same minimisation without
admissibility, so $L \le E$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 7.1" >}} Under (S) and (A1),
$\mathcal F = \{(E(T), 2T) : T \in \mathbb N,\ E(T) < E(T-1)\}$ with $E(-1) = \infty$, makespans in
units of $g$.
:::

The Pareto front is read off the levels where $E$ drops, and only a bounded range of levels
matters.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 7.10" >}} **Ends of the front.** Assume (S), and let
$d_{\min} = \min_i d_i$, $c_{\min} = \min_i c_i$ and $d_{\rm cheap} = \min\{d_i : c_i = c_{\min}\}$.

*(a)* Every plan has makespan at least $2 d_{\min}\kappa$, and some plan attains it.

*(b)* Every plan costs at least $(2t - p)\,c_{\min}$, and $((2t - p)\,c_{\min},\ 2 d_{\rm cheap}\kappa)$
is the cheapest point of $\mathcal F$.

*(c)* With integer durations, $E(T) < \infty$ if and only if $T \ge T_{\rm lo} := d_{\min}\kappa$,
and $E(T) = (2t - p)\,c_{\min}$ if and only if $T \ge T_{\rm hi} := d_{\rm cheap}\kappa$. The same
holds for $L$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* $p$ non-empty groups of total size $2t - p$ include one of size at least
$\kappa = \lceil (2t - p)/p \rceil$, which gives both lower bounds through Lemma 3.4; they are
attained by spreading $2t - p$ copies of one city over the planes, which is admissible by
{{< node "Lemma 2.9" >}} ({{< node "Proposition 7.10" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

On the [example instance](#fig-plan) ($2t - p = 4$, $\kappa = 2$,
$d_{\min} = 2$, $d_{\rm cheap} = 5$), the levels run from $T_{\rm lo} = 4$ to $T_{\rm hi} = 10$:

| $T$ | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $E(T)$ | 36 | 30 | 24 | 20 | 14 | 14 | 4 |
| front point | $(36, 8)$ | $(30, 10)$ | $(24, 12)$ | $(20, 14)$ | $(14, 16)$ | none | $(4, 20)$ |

: $E$ on the example instance, computed by enumeration; $L = E$ at every level. Level 9 is not a breakpoint, so the front has no point of makespan 18. {#tbl-levels}

A city dominated by another can be removed ({{< node "Proposition 7.9" >}}): if
$d_{i'} \le d_i$ and $c_{i'} \le c_i$, removing $i$ changes neither $E$ nor $L$ at any level, nor
the front. The kept cities have increasing durations and decreasing costs.

**One-plane table.** Everything is built from the cheapest group of a single plane.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 7.2" >}} Let $G[0][\tau] = 0$ for $\tau \ge 0$,
$G[m][\tau] = \min_{i : d_i \le \tau}\big(c_i + G[m-1][\tau - d_i]\big)$, and $G[m][\tau] = \infty$
for $\tau < 0$. Then $G[m][\tau]$ is the least cost of a multiset of $m$ cities of total duration
at most $\tau$.
:::

**Bounds.** Bounds on $E(T)$ combine *gadgets*, small sets of planes with their groups, by a
knapsack over planes and landings. Single planes of any size give $L$. Single planes of odd size
and *pairs*, two even planes linked by one $(B\bar B)$-pairing, give an upper bound $U$; adding
*chains* of three planes, even, odd and even, gives $U_3$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 7.3" >}} $L(T) \le E(T) \le U_3(T) \le U(T)$.
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 7.4" >}} If $q_{\max} \le 2$, that is $p \le 2$ or $t \le p + 1$, then
$E = U$. If $q_{\max} \le 3$, that is $p \le 3$ or $t \le p + 2$, then $E = U_3$.
:::

Every gadget with optimal groups is a tree of a link forest; when the trees of every link forest
have at most two or three planes ({{< node "Corollary 2.7" >}}), the gadgets cover all of them.
Pairs alone are not always enough: for three planes and the list of durations
$\{4, 4, 2, 6, 6, 6, 7\}$, the groups $\{6, 6\}$, $\{4, 7\}$ and $\{4, 2, 6\}$ reach makespan 24,
the two even groups sharing no city and being linked through the odd one, a chain; pairs reach
only 26.

**The link-forest dynamic program.** When the bracket $L \le E \le U_3$ does not close, $E(T)$ is
computed exactly by building the trees of a link forest from the leaves up: a table of child
items (a pairing with the subtree hanging from it), a table of subtrees hanging from a parent
pairing, a table of rooted trees, and a knapsack that combines trees into a forest of $p$ planes
and $2t - p$ landings, the free landings of each plane being filled from $G$. By Corollary 2.7,
trees never need more than $q_{\max}$ planes.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 7.5" >}} The link-forest dynamic program returns $E(T)$. Given $G$, it takes
$O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2 T + p\,q_{\max} s^2)$ time and $O(q_{\max} s T + n\,q_{\max} s + p s)$ memory
per level, with $s = 2t - p$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Every finite entry is the cost of a structure satisfying (F1) and (F2), whose groups
are admissible by {{< node "Lemma 2.6" >}}; conversely, the rooted link forest of an optimal
partition is bounded below entry by entry
({{< node "Theorem 7.5" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

Over the levels $[T_{\rm lo}, T_{\rm hi}]$, with $G$ built once in $O(n\,s\,T_{\rm hi})$, the
whole front takes $O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2\,T_{\rm hi}(T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo} + 1))$ time, which is
pseudo-polynomial since $T_{\rm hi} \le d_{\max}\kappa$.

**The σ-DP.** A second exact program works on parity matrices directly. By
{{< node "Lemma 2.8" >}}, an admissible partition of $2t - p$ cities has a parity matrix touching
at most $w = \min(p - 1, t - p)$ cities. The *σ-graph* has nodes $(k, j, \sigma)$: $k$ planes
processed, $j$ landings used, and $\sigma$ the set of cities marked an odd number of times so far,
of size at most $w$. An arc adds a plane with $m$ landings and a set $\eta$ of marked cities,
weighted by $c(\eta)$ plus the cheapest filler from $G$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 7.6" >}} **σ-DP.** The shortest path from $(0, 0, \emptyset)$ to
$(p, 2t - p, \emptyset)$ in the σ-graph has weight $E(T)$.
:::

The σ-DP is polynomial in $n$ for fixed $w$; the link-forest program is the default otherwise.
Replacing arc weights by finite Pareto sets of (cost, duration) pairs
({{< node "Lemma 7.7" >}}) gives a variant that computes the whole front in one pass
({{< node "Proposition 7.8" >}}); it helps when durations are large and the range of costs is
narrow.

**Constructing the plan.** For each front point, a partition attaining $E(T)$ is rebuilt from the
choices of the exact program, a link forest is computed from it as in the proof of Lemma 2.6, and
the plan is built as in {{< node "Theorem 4.1" >}}.

**Complexity.**

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Corollary 8.3" >}} $E(T)$, and under (S) and (A1) the Pareto front, are computable in
pseudo-polynomial time. So computing the front is not strongly NP-hard unless P = NP.
:::

Whether deciding $E(T) \le C$ is NP-hard, with $t$ written in unary as in PDDL, is open. The
per-level costs of each step, with $\hat m = s - p + 1$ the largest group size and
$N_w = \sum_{u \le \lfloor 3w/2 \rfloor} \binom{n}{u} 3^u$, are as follows.

| Step | Time | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| One-plane table $G$, all levels | $O(n\,\hat m\,T_{\rm hi})$ | $O(\hat m\,T_{\rm hi})$ |
| $L$ and $U$, per level | $O(p\,s^2 + n\,\hat m^2)$ | $O(p\,s + \hat m^2)$ |
| $U_3$ chains, per level | $O(n^2\,\hat m\,s + p\,s^2)$ | $O(p\,s)$ |
| Link-forest DP, per level | $O(n\,q_{\max}^2 s^2 T + p\,q_{\max} s^2)$ | $O(q_{\max} s T + n\,q_{\max} s)$ |
| σ-DP, per level | $O(p\,s\,\hat m\,N_w)$ | $O(s\sum_{u \le w}\binom{n}{u})$ per layer |
| Plan for one point | $O(s + n + p)$, up to union-find | $O(s + n + p)$ |

: Complexity of the steps, with $s = 2t - p$. For all levels, multiply by $T_{\rm hi} - T_{\rm lo} + 1$. {#tbl-complexity}

### ZenoSolver {#sec-zenosolver}

ZenoSolver is a C++ software dedicated to generate and exactly solve MultiZenoTravel instances.
ZenoSolver computes the true Pareto Front using the algorithm described in this section. It
outputs the corresponding PDDL file, that can be directly used by most AI planners.

For a symmetric instance, it reduces the instance (gcd of the durations, dominated cities),
computes $T_{\rm lo}$, $T_{\rm hi}$ and $G$, evaluates $L$ and $U$ on every level, refines with
$U_3$ where they differ, and runs an exact program only on the levels the bracket leaves open. As
$E$ is non-increasing, $E(a) = E(b)$ for $a < b$ fixes $E$ on $[a, b]$, which allows bisection
over runs of open levels. A plan is then built and simulated for every front point. For a
non-symmetric instance, it brackets the front between lower bounds and achieved plans, and closes
the gaps by a search over role configurations, as described in the
[non-symmetric section](#sec-ns-front).

With each front, ZenoSolver can write a certificate that a checker verifies without trusting it,
and the Lean development contains a solver of its own, proved correct
([Verification](#sec-verification)). The experiment [E7](#sec-e7) and the
[benchmark suites](#sec-bench) report the performances of the C++ solver.

### Certificates {#sec-certificates}

A Pareto front is a strong claim: no plan, among infinitely many, beats any of its points. A
certificate reduces the claim to finitely many checks that a program much simpler than the solver
can run. For a symmetric instance and a list $(C_1, M_1), \dots, (C_r, M_r)$ with
$M_1 < \dots < M_r$ and $C_1 > \dots > C_r$, a checker verifies four obligations:

1. every listed point has a plan, which the checker simulates: feasible, of cost $C_i$ and
   makespan $M_i$;
2. no plan has makespan below $M_1$: the checker verifies $M_1 = 2 d_{\min}\kappa$;
3. for every $i < r$, every plan of makespan below $M_{i+1}$ costs at least $C_i$: the checker
   establishes a lower bound of at least $C_i$ at the level
   $T^\star_i = \lfloor \lfloor (M_{i+1} - 1)/2 \rfloor / g \rfloor$;
4. no plan costs less than $C_r$: the checker verifies $C_r = (2t - p)\,c_{\min}$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 9.1" >}} **End to end.** If obligations 1 to 4 hold, then
$\mathcal F = \{(C_i, M_i) : 1 \le i \le r\}$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Every point of $\mathcal A$ lies at or after $M_1$, so it falls in some interval
$[M_i, M_{i+1})$ or after $M_r$, where obligation 3 or 4 bounds its cost by $C_i$; the list is
therefore a finite dominating subset, and {{< node "Lemma 1.1" badge=false >}} applies
({{< node "Theorem 9.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

The work of the checker is obligation 3. A gap of kind `relaxed` recomputes $L(T^\star_i)$, which
is sound under (S) alone by Lemma 3.4, whatever the flights between central cities. A gap of kind
`forest` recomputes $E(T^\star_i)$ with the checker's own link-forest program, which is sound
under (A1) by Theorem 4.7 and under (AΔ) by Theorem 4.10. On 400 random instances, all but 15 of
5,277 gaps close with `relaxed`, so 386 of the 400 fronts are certified by the relaxation alone.
Two further kinds are proved sound but are not part of the format: `gadget`, which recomputes $U$
or $U_3$ where Proposition 7.4 makes them exact, and `sigma-potential`, a sparse dual certificate
for the σ-DP built from {{< node "Lemma 9.2" >}} and {{< node "Lemma 9.3" >}}.

For non-symmetric instances the format has a version 2, whose gap kinds rest on the results of
the [non-symmetric section](#sec-nonsymmetric): `relaxed`, `roles`, `lagrangian`, `balanced`, and
`search` for the gaps that waiting leaves open. The
[certificate format](../solver/certificates.qmd) page describes the files.

#### Verification {#sec-verification}

A certificate moves the trust from the solver to the checker, and the checker to a theorem.
Two checkers implement the obligations: `zeno check`, in C++, and `zeno-check`, compiled from
Lean. Both print the assumptions a certificate relied on, among (S), (A1) or (AΔ), and (A1-NS).

**The Lean checker.** Its soundness is the theorem `Cert.check_sound`: if `Cert.check` accepts a
certificate of format version 1, the listed points are exactly the Pareto front of the instance,
over every feasible plan. It holds for any flights between central cities when all gaps are
`relaxed` (`Cert.check_sound_relaxed`), for flights satisfying (A1) through Theorem 4.7
(`Cert.check_sound_A1`), and for flights satisfying (AΔ) through Theorem 4.10
(`Cert.check_sound_ATri`); variants cover rational times and planes ending anywhere
(`Cert.check_sound_rat`, `Cert.check_sound_anywhere`). For version 2, `Cert2.check_sound` holds
for every table of central flights satisfying (A1-NS) when the certificate lists that
assumption, and for every table otherwise ({{< node "Version 2 checker" >}}). On the 66
certificates the C++ solver writes for the benchmark suite, up to 3.9 MB and 240,000 legs, the
compiled Lean checker accepts every one, in 33 ms at the median and 2.3 s at most.

**The verified solver.** `zeno-front` is a solver of its own, written in Lean, with a proof that
its output is the Pareto front ({{< node "Verified solver" >}}): `solveFront_isParetoFront` under
(S) and (A1), and `solveFront_isParetoFront_ATri` under (S) and (AΔ), for $1 \le p \le t$. It
finds the levels where $E$ drops by splitting intervals between $d_{\min}\kappa$ and
$(2t - p)\,d_{\max}$, takes $L(T)$ wherever the bracket $L \le E \le U$ closes
(`minCost_eq_of_bracket`), and otherwise runs the σ-DP or the
link-forest program, whose exactness is `sigmaBoundAt_eq_minCost` (Theorem 7.6) and
`treeBoundAt_eq_minCost` (Theorem 7.5). It solves the 66 instances of the benchmark suite, 0.04 s
at the median and 10 s at most, and its fronts equal those of the C++ solver, which continuous
integration checks on the golden instances.

**What is trusted.** A machine-checked statement is a Lean theorem whose axioms are among
`propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, which an audit of every declaration reads when the
site is built. The executables add the Lean compiler and the code that parses the files, which is
not verified. The badges of this paper come from that audit. Among the results of the
non-symmetric section, Theorems 6.1 and 6.9 are machine-checked as well; its examples and
propositions, and those of the general section, are proved in the theory note or computed. The
experiment [E8](#sec-e8) tests
both checkers against thousands of corrupted certificates.
